extraction.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
extraction.document_type: Working paper, formal theory (manuscript dated February 2024, 10,328 words). The text names no journal or publisher.
extraction.identification: Not applicable: no estimation or causal identification. Claims are model-internal comparative statics. The authors call for future empirical work to test the predictions (p.5, p.25-26).
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1613 lines of the extracted text, including title, abstract, introduction, related literature, model (Sec. 1), equilibrium (Sec. 2), dynamics (Sec. 3), electoral-strength extension (Sec. 4), conclusion (Sec. 5), references, and Online Appendix A.1-A.4. Page numbers cited are the manuscript's printed footers. All 118 of Paul's highlights were read from the single annotation file. The text does not discuss networks, lobbying, path-finding, allocation, or text measurement, and has no election data, so those topics are absent by design rather than skipped.
extraction.research_question: How can presidential leadership, specifically going public, both raise issue salience to move Congress toward the president's policy and increase legislative polarization? And how does this tension shape a president's decision to go public in the first place? (p.1-2)
extraction.theory: Going public raises issue salience and activates party bases, which pressure co-partisan and out-partisan legislators (Canes-Wrone 2006 versus Lee 2009's partisan retreat). The model combines pivotal-politics bargaining (Krehbiel 1998; Dziuda and Loeper 2018; Gehlbach 2021) with a partisan president whose reelection is tied to the policy outcome. Party branding and legislative-cartel logic (Cox and McCubbins 2005, 2007) motivates "defensive appeals," where the president goes public to deter co-partisan defection rather than to persuade out-partisans. Sincere polarization (z) and strategic polarization from base pressure (beta) and electoral stakes (delta) are manipulated separately (p.5-6, p.10-11).
extraction.data: None. This is a formal model with no sample, unit, period, or N. Empirical material is limited to illustrations: Biden's 2023 debt-ceiling remarks (p.2), Biden's COVID emergency and abortion appeals (p.3, p.23), Trump's ACA repeal attempt (p.24), and a Pew 2019 poll showing a partisan gap of seven points on infrastructure versus 46 on health care (p.22). These are cited as illustrations, not tested.
extraction.method: Game-theoretic model. Pure-strategy subgame perfect equilibrium solved by backward induction (p.11, p.13). Players are a president P, a left party L, a right party R, and a non-strategic challenger. The preference shock is theta ~ Uniform[-psi, psi]. Gridlock regions and cost thresholds for going public (c(1), c(-1)) are derived in closed form (Prop. 1-2, App. A.1-A.2). Comparative statics are reported as propositions (Prop. 3-5). Figures 1, 3, 4, and 5 give numerical illustrations at stated parameter values. Section 4 extends the model so the president's silent-reelection probability rho(x_sq) differs by status quo (Prop. 6, App. A.4).
extraction.scope: Contemporary US presidency and two-party Congress with separation of powers, as motivated by 2021-2023 examples. The model covers one binary policy dimension, one issue, and two veto pivots (one per party). The president has no formal agenda power (p.4). The authors note the framework could also fit a mid-twentieth-century "golden age" of less polarized parties (p.23). Single-issue and single-dimension scope is stated as a limitation (p.31).

key_findings.finding: Going public always widens the gridlock region, even when both party bases rally behind the president. Silent gridlock region is (-z, z). Public gridlock region is bounded by (-z + beta_R - delta)/2 and (z + beta_L + delta)/2 (bar notation on beta lost in extraction). Asymmetric base influence drives this 'effective polarization.'
key_findings.location: Prop. 1 (p.13); Fig. 1 and note (p.14); proof in App. A.1 (p.38)
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 1 illustrative values: z = 1; beta_L > 0 = 0.75; beta_L < 0 = -0.5; beta_R > 0 = 0.5; beta_R < 0 = -0.75; delta = 0.5

key_findings.finding: Going public can raise presidential legislative success, not only polarization, because co-partisans move further toward the president than out-partisans under a Rally. This harmonizes Canes-Wrone (2006) with Lee (2009).

The president goes public for a wider range of opportunity costs when the status quo is favorable: c(-1) > c(1) always. Three regions result: c <= c(1) always goes public; c in (c(1), c(-1)] goes public only if status quo favorable; c > c(-1) never goes public.
key_findings.numbers: c(-1) - c(1) is shown to be positive for 0<p<1, 0<q<1, ps i > z > 0, delta > 0 (App. A.2, p.40)

key_findings.finding: Defensive appeal: under Partisan Retreat (q = 1), the president never goes public when the status quo is unfavorable (c_q(1) strictly negative), but always has an incentive to go public when the status quo is favorable (c_q(-1) strictly positive).

Under Backfire (1-p-q = 1), the president never goes public with an unfavorable status quo (c_b(1) = c_q(1)). With a favorable status quo she sometimes profits from going public even though it is certain to backfire. The threshold is beta_L < -delta(delta + 2z + 2) / (2(delta + 2)), which falls as z and delta rise.

Rally Around the President (p = 1): c_p(-1) and c_p(1) rise with the out-party base's support beta_R (for unfavorable status quo). The gap c_p(-1) - c_p(1) falls as beta_R rises. c_p(1) need not be positive, so the president may not go public even under the most favorable base reactions, because a high delta lets the out-party resist.

Prop. 3 (beliefs about reactions): c(1) increases in p; c(-1) increases in p and in q. Higher Backlash probability (1-p-q) reduces going public when the status quo is favorable. When unfavorable, Backlash or Retreat matters only if it comes at the expense of p.
key_findings.numbers: dc(1)/dp = (beta_R-bar - beta_R)(2+delta)/(2psi) > 0; dc(-1)/dq > 0 (sign as in proof)

key_findings.finding: Prop. 4 (legislative polarization z): going public becomes more likely with favorable status quo and less likely with unfavorable status quo as z rises.
key_findings.location: Prop. 4 (p.25); discussion of cross-sectional predictions (p.25-26); proof App. A.3.2 (p.42)
key_findings.numbers: dc(-1)/dz = delta/(2psi) > 0; dc(1)/dz = -delta/(2psi) < 0; d(Delta c)/dz = delta/psi > 0

key_findings.finding: Prop. 5 (policy uncertainty psi): the president is weakly less likely to go public as psi rises. The gap between favorable and unfavorable thresholds shrinks as psi rises, so the president's behavior is less sensitive to the status quo under high uncertainty.

Electoral strength extension: higher silent-reelection probability rho lowers the go-public range (Eqs. 12, 14). If rho(-1) > rho(1) and psi is large (psi > psi*, Eq. 15), the ordering of thresholds can flip so the president goes public more under an unfavorable status quo ('gambling for reelection', after Downs and Rocke 1994).

Illustrative empirical gap: Biden's 2021 infrastructure law fits the case of elite polarization exceeding mass polarization (z > 0, beta_R = beta_R-bar). The authors cite a Pew 2019 partisan gap of seven points on infrastructure versus 46 on health care. This is an illustration, not a test.
key_findings.numbers: partisan gap 7 points (infrastructure) vs 46 points (health care), Pew Research Center 2019

limitations: Stated by the authors: the election is blunt. The president wins or loses with certainty given the policy outcome, which ignores other electoral factors (p.30).
Stated: the model covers a single issue and a single dimension. Presidents strategically choose among issues and rhetorical arguments, which the model does not capture (p.30-31).
Stated: the model is policy-focused. A president may go public to signal commitment and mobilize a core constituency even when that dampens passage prospects (p.30).
Stated: the lack of party labels leaves open who the representative legislator and voter are (p.6). The two veto pivots are modeled as party representatives (fn. 4, p.8).
Stated: a Backfire is rarely observed, which may be endogenous to whether presidents raise salience on unpopular issues (p.24).
Stated: if z < psi, no preference shock could ever lead the parties to agree, so going public would never matter. The authors set this case aside (fn. 5, p.8).
Stated: the reelection probability after staying silent is fixed at 1/2 in the main model. Section 4 relaxes this (p.10, p.28).
Stated: the empirical implications (partisan gap, status quo, uncertainty) are not tested with data. The paper gives only illustrative examples.
Stated: several comparative statics hold only weakly, since cost thresholds can be negative and then parameter changes have no effect on behavior (fn. 10, p.18; App. A.3).
measures: Model primitives, not empirical measures: z (sincere/ideological polarization, common knowledge); psi (bound on preference shock, i.e., policy uncertainty); delta (reelection/co-partisan payoff); c (cost of going public); p, q, and 1-p-q (probabilities of Rally, Partisan Retreat, Backfire); beta_L and beta_R (party-base pressure, with upper and lower bounds); rho(x_sq) (silent-reelection probability). Status quo x_sq in {-1, 1}. Table 1 (p.8-9) gives the joint distribution of base reactions.

summary_md:
Noble and Turner build a formal model with no data. A partisan president decides whether to "go public" on one binary issue before two party pivots vote. Going public activates both party bases. The bases then rally, retreat (co-partisans move toward the president, out-partisans away) or backfire. It also ties the president's reelection to the outcome, which gives co-partisans an electoral stake (delta).

Results:
- Going public always widens the gridlock interval (Prop 1).
- Because the status quo matters, presidents go public over a wider range of costs when the status quo already favors them (c(-1) > c(1), Prop 2). The authors call this a "defensive appeal" aimed at fair-weather co-partisans.
- Under partisan retreat the president never goes public against an unfavorable status quo.
- Higher sincere polarization (z) makes going public more attractive in defense and less attractive on offense (Prop 4).
- Higher uncertainty (psi) weakly reduces going public and blunts its sensitivity to the status quo (Prop 5).
- The authors propose these as predictions to test. Nothing in the paper estimates them.

This matters because Melange implements the paper almost line for line in fec/engine/salience_shock.py and the dashboard's exec cue. The party asymmetry carries over faithfully. Several mappings do not. The estimator ties rally and retreat odds to the elite stance gap, psi is built from missing stance data, and the paper's presidential-reelection channel is moved onto legislators and onto a CU advocacy actor.

The sharpest problem is in the live advisory. It credits "defections prevented" on every issue, whatever its status quo, so its four GO PUBLIC verdicts (written 2026-10-08) all fall on offense issues. That reverses the paper's central prediction. This finding comes from one agent analysis path and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Going public is more attractive when the status quo is favorable: c(-1) > c(1) always (Prop 2). Under Partisan Retreat the president never goes public against an unfavorable status quo (c_q(1) < 0) but always has an incentive to defend a favorable one. The model predicts that going public occurs more often in defense of a favorable status quo than to win policy change (p.26). The defensive appeal logic depends on the co-partisan being the relevant pivot, which holds only when the status quo is favorable (p.17, p.24).
bearings.paper_location: Eqs. 7-8 and Prop. 2 (p.16-17); Partisan Retreat (p.22-23); p.26; App. A.2 (p.39-40)
bearings.system_side: defensive_appeal_value() runs for every issue with no status-quo check. The advisory value is E_dspread + 1.5 x len(defections_prevented) for offense and defend issues alike. In the live salience_advisory.json (2026-10-08 15:37, 18 issues), the four GO PUBLIC verdicts (top quartile, cut 68.27) are all sq=offense, and each is driven by held counts: Technology & Emerging (E_dspread -3.87, held 67, q=0.83), Member Business Lending (+5.83, held 60), Data Privacy (-19.35, held 68) and Fraud Prevention (-9.73, held 52). The three defend issues rank 13th to 15th. Tech & Emerging is close to the paper's pure-retreat case on an unfavorable status quo, where the paper says never go public, yet it is ranked first. The dashboard bundle surfaces these verdicts as 'GO PUBLIC · holds N'. UNVERIFIED single-path analysis (DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: No empirical transfer is needed. This is an internal-consistency check against the model the code claims to implement. The contradiction holds whenever the defensive credit is added on sq='offense' issues. Gating held to sq=='defend' would restore the paper's ordering. Whether the paper's ordering is right for a CU advocacy campaign is a separate, untested question.

bearings.system_side: salience_issue_params estimates z as the absolute D-R gap in mean legislator stance tier. It then sets q = (1-b) x min(1, z/3) and p = (1-b)(1 - z/3). The elite stance gap therefore sets the mass-base reaction odds. The resulting regime mixture drives both the advisory and the dashboard exec cue.

That would need a base-side or mass-opinion measure, such as a partisan gap in public or credit-union-member opinion per issue, which the system does not have. The paper's own example warns that the two can diverge.

bearings.paper_claim: There are three base-reaction regimes: Rally (both toward), Partisan Retreat (co toward, out away) and Backfire (both away, out more). The single restriction is beta_L > beta_R: co-partisans always favor the president's proposal more than out-partisans do. Going public adds the electoral stake delta to the thresholds as (z + beta_L + delta)/2 and (-z + beta_R - delta)/2.

extraction.theory: Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky 1979; cumulative version Tversky & Kahneman 1992) versus expected utility theory. Tested regularities: probability weighting (overweighting of small probabilities, underweighting of large ones), the common ratio effect (Allais), the reflection effect (risk seeking for losses, risk aversion for gains, via probability weighting and diminishing sensitivity), loss aversion, and the reference-point dependence of risk attitudes. Risk is defined as outcome variance (p.104).
extraction.data: Sample: 46 sitting Dutch MPs in the lower chamber (Tweede Kamer), about 30% of parliament (p.103, p.107). Unit: individual MP. Period: sessions from September 2014 to January 2015, with no elections or major political events in that window (p.107). Sample traits: 28% female, 81% university-educated, mean age 43.5, 76.2% describe themselves as (very) right-wing (p.107). Lottery-valuation tasks use n = 28 (Table 2, p.109); the pooled political-scenario logistic regression uses n = 164 (Table 5, p.112). The text does not explain why 164 rather than 46 x 4 = 184. Validation comparison: student sample n = 176 (Appendix E, not in file; also n = 102 for the incentivized subset of the student lottery-valuation tasks).
extraction.method: Lab-style online experiment, individually completed with at least one researcher present (p.107). Thirteen decision tasks in three parts, with part order and task order within parts randomized (p.107). Part I: six lottery-choice tasks (common ratio tasks 1-2, reflection tasks 5-6, and others) testing EUT deviations. Part II: three lottery-valuation tasks using a multiple-price list (p.109). Part III: four hypothetical political scenarios, each with a gain or loss frame (p.111). Task-related incentives: one randomly selected task (from the lottery-choice or lottery-valuation part) determines a donation to one of seven charities (p.107). For loss frames, the maximum possible loss is added to the donation so that gain and loss frames have identical payoffs (p.109). Analysis: binomial tests (Tables 1 and 3), Fisher's exact tests (Table 4), and logistic regression with robust standard errors clustered by individual (Table 5, p.112).
extraction.identification: Within-subject randomized framing. Reflection tasks 5 and 6 hold final outcomes equal by adding EUR 60 to task 6 (p.110). Political scenarios use earlier expectations so that absolute outcomes match across frames (p.111). summary_md:
Linde and Vis ran an incentivized online experiment with 46 sitting Dutch MPs in 2014-2015, about 30% of the Tweede Kamer. They asked whether politicians depart from expected utility theory the way prospect theory predicts.

**What holds up**
- **Reflection effect in the paid lottery task.** The risky option was chosen by 39.1% under a gain frame and 76.1% under a loss frame (p = 0.0002, n = 46).
- **Asian disease problem.** The risky option was chosen by 88.5% under a loss frame and 30% under a gain frame (odds ratio 14.6).

**What does not hold up**
- **Political scenarios.** Reflection appears only in the scenario where votes and economic outcomes are both at stake: 85% vs 69%, Fisher p = 0.30. It reaches 5% significance only when all four scenarios are pooled (odds ratio 8.68, p = 0.033, n = 164 rather than the expected 184, which is unexplained). That pooled figure combines scenario types, three of which show no effect. On this basis the authors say, as suggestive evidence, that votes rather than policy set politicians' reference point.
- **Other effects.** No common ratio effect was found. The lottery-valuation tasks (n = 28) show nothing significant. Neither sample shows loss aversion (fn 4, p.105). Age, tenure, sex and ideology predict nothing.
- **"Smaller than other people."** This claim rests on comparison with earlier literature, not on a test in the main text.

**Why it matters here**
Melange cites this paper twice:
- **Receptivity layer.** Members in a live race are put in a "loss domain" with pt_mult 1.15, and safe members get 0.92.
- **Money response.** LOSSFRAME = 1.10 makes competitor money move a member's lean more than equal CU money. The comment describes this as loss aversion "elite-attenuated per Linde-Vis".

The paper supports the reflection effect itself. It does not support:
- loss aversion, which it did not find;
- treating seat insecurity as a loss frame, since framing was randomly manipulated and Dutch MPs are elected from national party lists, not single-member seats;
- equating risk-seeking (preferring higher-variance outcomes) with being easier to move by money;
- any of the constants 1.15, 0.92 or 1.10.

bearings.system_side: pt_domain = loss if the member has a defend or contest electoral play, or security < 0.45. pt_mult = 1.15 for loss ('gambles under threat, more movable') and 0.92 for gain. It enters pressure_mult = clip(susc_mult x incent x pt, 0.50, 1.60), which scales the money terms in shift_lean and in pflip. The docstring also says politicians are 'loss-averse overall'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: What carries over: the reflection effect is real in politicians, and electoral stakes (votes) are the more plausible reference dimension, which fits keying the domain on a live race. What does not: (a) framing was randomly assigned in hypothetical scenarios, not inferred from a member's seat security, so the paper never shows that safe-seat members sit in a gain domain. (b) The sample is Dutch list-PR MPs from 2014-2015 with no single-member seats, so seat-level competitiveness has no analogue. (c) Risk-seeking means preferring higher-variance options. The paper does not show it makes a member more responsive to money or pressure, the use pt_mult is put to. (d) The 1.15/0.92 magnitudes and the 'loss-averse overall' line are not supported; the paper reports no loss aversion. Evidence for the political-scenario effect rests on one non-significant scenario and n=164 (46 MPs).

bearings.paper_claim: The political-scenario reflection effect is weak and limited to one scenario (85% vs 69.23%, p=0.302), and the paper reports no loss aversion. Effect direction for the pt domain is therefore uncertain, and the size of LOSSFRAME is unsupported.
bearings.system_side: The receptivity sensitivity sweep varies PT only from 1.15/0.92 to 1.10/0.95 (mild) and to 1.25/0.85 (strong). It has no PT-off (1.0/1.0) or reversed variant and does not sweep LOSSFRAME.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies directly. These are the constants whose literature support is weakest after reading the paper. Adding a pt = 1.0/1.0 arm and a LOSSFRAME = 1.0 arm to the existing top-20/50 overlap harness would show whether either constant changes targeting decisions. This is a diagnostic sweep, not a confirmatory look.

gaps_exposed: No measured reference point for members. The paper says the reference point is electoral (votes) and depends on earlier expectations. The system uses seat security or an electoral play as a fixed proxy for 'loss domain' and never models expectations, such as a member's prior margin or forecast swing.

The system has no evidence that risk-seeking in the paper's sense (choosing higher-variance outcomes) means being more responsive to money or pressure. pt_mult assumes that link, and nothing in the system tests it.

Domain-specific framing is missing. The paper finds reflection only when votes are at stake. The system applies one pt_mult to every CU issue, whether or not the issue carries electoral consequences for the member.

There is no ablation of the Linde-Vis constants. The sensitivity harness lacks a pt-off arm and a LOSSFRAME-off arm, so no one has checked whether these unsupported constants change targeting decisions.

Competitiveness is counted several times. Seat security drives incent_mult (neutralized under COMPET_MULT), the pt loss test (security<0.45 or a defend/contest play), and, per D-104, the Cook-PVI multiplier c. The paper gives no support for stacking an electoral-risk effect on top of a competitiveness effect.
flags: Misattribution in code: receptivity_layer.py:23 says politicians are 'loss-averse overall', and LOSSFRAME 1.10 (money_response.py:28-31, receptivity_layer.py:26-28) cites loss aversion 'elite-attenuated per Linde-Vis'. The paper found NO loss aversion in either sample (fn 4, p.105). audit_full.py:62-63 locks the asymmetry in as 'by design' with this citation.

The 'MPs' framing effects are smaller than students'' premise (receptivity_layer.py:28) is not tested directly in the main text. It comes from comparison with earlier literature, and the student data (Appendix E) is not in the file. The paid-lottery reflection effect among MPs is large: 36.96 pp.

Any quote of the pooled political-scenario loss-frame OR 8.684 (p=0.033) must carry the UNSTRATIFIED label or the per-scenario strata. Pooling spans scenario types, and three of the four show no effect. The n is 164, not 184, and the paper does not explain why.

Transfer limit: the sample is 46 Dutch list-PR MPs (76.2% right-wing) answering hypothetical scenarios that were not incentivized. Mapping their results onto US House and Senate seat security is an inference the paper does not test.
The paper does not argue for either of the rejected SNA proposals, and it makes no reciprocity, closeness or access claims. The brain wording rules are not triggered.
paul_alignment: Paul's 44 highlights cover the reflection effect ("politicians are very vulnerable to the framing of outcomes"), the result that votes rather than policy set the reference point, the social-desirability caveat, the missing common ratio effect, and the "somewhat smaller" deviations. Measured against the paper, his takeaway is accurate on reflection. His summary "weaker than in the public" repeats the authors' abstract, but that comparison is drawn from earlier literature and not tested in the main text. He did not highlight the loss-aversion null (fn 4), which is the finding that most undercuts the built system. His position for money-response-defection says his notes do not discuss defection mechanics, but the code cites this paper as the basis for LOSSFRAME. On that point the system goes further than both his notes and the paper. For receptivity-layer, his notes support the general idea (domain-dependent risk attitudes keyed to electoral stakes). They do not support treating seat insecurity as a loss frame, or the 1.15/0.92 constants. His notes are not stale. The system's citation of the paper overstates it.

related.why: The receptivity layer pairs the two papers as separate channels that read the same seat-security input (incent_mult from Fouirnaies & Hall, pt_mult from Linde & Vis). The code records the resulting security-squared component as a design choice (receptivity_layer.py:200-204).

salience_shock.py:56-60,104 amplifies members with a live race by 1.35 ('gambling for reelection', Noble A.4). Linde & Vis's suggestive finding that votes set the reference point is the individual-level, prospect-theory version of the same electoral-stakes idea.
Byrne's choking-under-pressure composite and Linde-Vis's pt domain are multiplied together in pressure_mult (receptivity_layer.py:227). Neither paper estimates the combined product.

backlinks.why: Linde and Vis motivate the receptivity layer's loss-domain term for members in a live race. Toss Up and Lean ratings are a direct marker of a live race.

extraction.title: A hypergraph analysis of the European Commission lobby network
extraction.venue: Applied Network Science, 10:45 (received 8 April 2025, accepted 22 August 2025). Metadata hint confirmed.
extraction.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), empirical network study
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in two chunks (lines 1-937, through the references and Publisher's Note), including abstract, introduction, results, discussion, methods, and references. Supplementary Information (SI tables 5, 8-14, Sections 4.1-13) is cited but not included in the text file, so SI-only content is not covered. All 41 annotation records in the annotation JSON were read; 38 are highlights with covered text and 3 are Ink marks with no covered text. Paul's annotations carry no sticky-note text, so every note field is empty.
extraction.research_question: Does a highly interconnected core of actors dominate the European Commission lobbying network (p.2)? What determines company centrality in that network (p.2, p.8), and do stakeholder categories (companies, trade associations, NGOs) differ in their core position (p.6-7)?
extraction.theory: Network theory of power concentration: core-periphery and rich-club structure as evidence of concentrated access and influence (p.2, p.4, p.10). Higher-order (hypergraph) theory: meetings are modeled as simultaneous multi-actor interactions because coordination among more than two actors matters (p.3). Centrality is treated as a proxy for embeddedness, not directly for influence (p.10). Interpretive concepts used in the discussion: Laurens' "bureaucratic capital" for business (p.7); Beyers and De Bruycker on NGO coalition-building and Hanegraaff and Pritoni on coalitions as a sign of weakness (p.7-8); "aggressive lobbying" (Kone and Farnhill 2019) (p.9).
extraction.data: Unit: a meeting (hyperedge) between EC officials (Commissioners, cabinet members, directors-general) and interest representatives. Node: an EC official or a stakeholder. Period: 1 Dec 2019 to 30 Nov 2024 (first von der Leyen Commission), from the EC meetings register (p.4, p.12). Full hypergraph H: |V| = 5,717 nodes and |E| = 18,561 hyperedges, including repeated multi-edges; one connected component (p.4). Stakeholder-only hypergraph Hstak: 43.32% of nodes in the largest component (p.4). Duplicate meetings merged with fuzzy partial-ratio >= 70, merging 460 pairs (p.12-13). Stakeholder attributes from the EU Transparency Register (data Jan 2017 to Jan 2024; 43 meeting identification codes not found; 34 duplicate names consolidated) (p.12-13). Firm financials and sector (NACE) from Bureau van Dijk Orbis, with a 93.9% match rate (p.13). Regression sample: companies, N = 1,178 in H and N = 702 in Hstak (p.8, Table 1).
extraction.method: Hypergraph construction from meeting co-attendance. Global structure: degree shares by stakeholder category, modularity (Louvain-type clustering, SI 8.4), edge-size and betweenness analysis, simpliciality (Landry et al. 2024) and edge entropy. Core-periphery: generalized normalized rich-club coefficient for hypergraphs, rho(k) = phi(k)/phi_rand(k), with phi_rand from six hypergraph configuration null models (Chodrow 2020), sampled by Metropolis-Hastings edge-swap rewiring (p.14-15). Hypercore decomposition (k,m) and hypercoreness centrality R(i) (Mancastroppa 2023, p.16). Core(r) composition by category for r where Core(r) is 10% to 1% of nodes (p.6-7). Comparison of hypercoreness with coreness on clique-expansion graphs (Pearson correlations, p.16-17). Regression: OLS of company hypercoreness on log FTE lobbying staff, log assets, binary levels of interest (European, global, national), EU head-office dummy, and NACE sector dummies (baseline C Manufacturing); coefficients standardized; skewed variables log-transformed; categories grouped; outliers removed (p.8-9, p.17-18).
extraction.identification: None. The OLS regression is cross-sectional and associational. The authors state the resource-centrality links "should not be read as one-way causal effects" and describe reverse causation (p.9). Robustness is checked through null models, multiedge versions and a regression on all stakeholder types (SI 8.6, p.10).
extraction.scope: Population: meetings disclosed by high-level EC officials, and the registered interest representatives who attended them. Institution: the European Commission only. The Council, European Parliament and other EU bodies are excluded (p.11). Era: 1 Dec 2019 to 30 Nov 2024 (first von der Leyen Commission). Core-periphery claims apply to the disclosed meetings, not to lobbying overall (p.10-11).

key_findings.finding: Global structure: the hypergraph is one connected component with heavy-tailed degrees; companies and groups account for 34.58% of stakeholder degree, trade and business associations 25.35%, NGOs 23.08%, all others 17.00%.
Meeting size and connectivity: most meetings are one-on-one, but large meetings are rare and key to connectivity. Edge betweenness correlates strongly with edge size.
key_findings.numbers: correlation 0.74 between edge betweenness and edge size

key_findings.finding: Siloed organization: the full network has strong community structure centred on individual Commissioners, so departments rarely share meetings.
key_findings.numbers: modularity 0.700

key_findings.finding: Stakeholder-only network is less connected. Its largest component holds 43.32% of nodes, with many small components. Meetings are homogeneous by stakeholder type. Meetings are more nested than random chance.
key_findings.numbers: largest component 43.32%; three simpliciality scores higher in the data than in size- and degree-preserving random hypergraphs (values in SI Fig. 14)

key_findings.finding: Rich-club among stakeholders: on the stakeholder-only hypergraph, rho(k) > 1 at all k under the stakeholder-only null models. The authors read this as persistent rich-club behaviour among stakeholders.
key_findings.numbers: rho(k) > 1 for all k

key_findings.finding: Full-network rich-club is not testable as stated: the full H lacks EC-only edges, which biases rho downward against null models that contain them. Under the hybrid null, the stakeholder rich-club is qualitatively present but less salient.
key_findings.numbers: rho < 1 for k > 10 under null models (1)-(2); hybrid null (3)-(4) quantitatively weaker

key_findings.finding: Core composition, full network: companies' share in the high-hypercoreness core rises above their graph share, and trade associations stay above their graph share. NGOs' share falls.
key_findings.numbers: core size shown for Core(r) at 10% to 1% of nodes

key_findings.finding: Core composition, stakeholder network: companies stay significant, NGOs' core share rises notably, and trade associations' share falls. NGOs are over-represented in the largest meetings and trade associations in the smallest.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; no NGO or association share values given in the text

key_findings.finding: Absence of research institutions: think tanks, research institutes and academic institutions are absent from the core of both networks.
key_findings.numbers: qualitative

key_findings.finding: Regression (companies, standardized OLS): FTE lobbying staff and assets are the strongest predictors in both networks. EU head office is strongly significant. Global and European interest levels are positive. National level is not significant.
Sector deviations from manufacturing: mining, energy and ICT companies are more central in the full network. Transport and finance are less central in the stakeholder-only network.

Hypercoreness versus clique coreness: the two clique-based measures correlate at r = 0.93 and the two hypergraph measures at r = 0.79. Cross-framework correlations are weaker. Clique projection inflates nodes that attend a few large meetings.
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.93 (clique pair); r = 0.79 (hypergraph pair)

key_findings.finding: Authors' policy reading: concentration of access among business actors, limited civil-society access to economic issues, and resource-driven centrality suggest a consultation process that is potentially biased and unequal. They also flag compartmentalization across departments.
key_findings.numbers: none

limitations: Centrality is not influence. The authors say network centrality does not directly measure influence, and cite prior work that links central positions to influence (p.10).
Cross-sectional OLS shows associations only; resources and centrality may cause each other (p.9).
Full-network rich-club cannot be tested against EC-only edges, because H has none (p.14).
Results depend on multi-edge treatment: with repeated meetings the core fragments at higher orders, so the analysis uses versions without multi-edges (p.5-6).
Duplicate detection uses a fuzzy-match threshold of 70, chosen by manual inspection of 60 to 100 pairs (p.12-13).

Register linkage is imperfect: 43 identification codes were not found, and the register is used only for the most recent entry (p.12-13). Orbis match rate is 93.9%, with manual checks for lower-confidence matches (p.13).
Scope is the EC only, excluding the Council and Parliament (p.11).
NGO coalition interpretation is uncertain. Meeting-initiation dynamics would be needed to establish the mechanism (p.8).
The regression covers companies only; NGOs and associations are analysed descriptively (p.8, p.10).
The authors say findings on the representativeness of large firms (0.02% of EU businesses, 38% of workforce) raise questions but are not tested (p.9).

summary_md:
Azaiez and Mandel model five years of disclosed European Commission meetings (Dec 2019 to Nov 2024) as a hypergraph. Each meeting is one hyperedge joining officials and stakeholders, giving 5,717 nodes and 18,561 meetings. The hypergraph is one connected component and splits into Commissioner-centred silos (modularity 0.700). Most meetings are one-on-one. The rare large meetings hold the network together: edge betweenness correlates 0.74 with meeting size.

Among stakeholders only, a size- and degree-preserving null model shows a rich club at every degree k. The full network cannot be tested the same way, because it has no official-only meetings to compare against. A hypercore decomposition puts companies and trade associations in the core of the full network and NGOs in the core of the stakeholder-only network. In a standardized OLS over 1,178 companies (R2 0.398), hypercoreness rises with lobbying FTE (0.464) and assets (0.253). The authors say this is association only, with reverse causation possible.

The most portable result for Paul is methodological. Projecting meetings onto pairwise cliques inflates nodes that attend a few large meetings. Coreness on the clique projection agrees only weakly with coreness on the hypergraph; within each framework the two measures correlate at 0.93 and 0.79. Melange builds two clique-style projections of group events: cosponsor rosters, and staffer payroll containers. The cosponsor network already discounts big bills by 1/sqrt(C). The staffer co-tenure operator has an open owner ruling on container-size normalization, and the paper's inflation finding is direct evidence for that ruling. It also helps explain the recorded r = 0.87 between staffer degree and office size.

The paper also says centrality measures embeddedness, not influence, and that resources drive it. This fits the system's retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar and D-025's wording rule. The paper's own Discussion slips into "access and influence" language, which must not carry over. The paper's edges come from a register that names both parties to each contact. US LD-2 filings do not, so this design cannot be reproduced with LDA data (D-021).

bearings.paper_claim: Projecting group interactions onto pairwise cliques inflates nodes that attend a few large meetings. Clique-based coreness agrees with clique-based coreness at r = 0.93 and hypercoreness with hypercoreness at r = 0.79, but agreement across the two frameworks is weaker. Separately, large meetings carry connectivity: edge betweenness correlates 0.74 with meeting size.
bearings.system_side: The co-tenure operator enumerates every concurrent pair inside a payroll container, which is a clique expansion of a container hyperedge. kappa depends only on container KIND. The 54 admin containers, which carried 70.8% of pairs in v5, were excluded by owner ruling 2026-09-07. Normalizing by container size is still an OPEN ruling: 'should an edge formed inside a 3,373-person container be down-weighted relative to one formed inside a 4-person office?'. The brain records degree vs largest office size r = 0.87.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The mechanism carries over: clique projection of any large hyperedge inflates its members. The magnitudes do not. EC meetings are single simultaneous events, while payroll containers are co-presence over years. The paper offers hypergraph-native measures (hypercoreness), not per-edge down-weighting, as its fix. The project's Katz finding (STATE.md:912-915) is that per-edge reweighting cannot remove a degree artifact under sum-based centrality. This is evidence for Paul's open ruling, not a recommendation.

bearings.paper_claim: Coordination inside a multi-actor interaction is not the same as having n-1 pairwise ties. Treating a large meeting as a full clique over-credits its attendees relative to repeated small meetings.
bearings.system_side: The exposure index already divides each shared day by concurrent headcount, using duration / max(1, count-1)^gamma in the Census prefix integrals. In the sidecar closeness math, a pair's contact opportunity therefore shrinks as the container grows, unlike the operator's kind-only kappa.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports the direction of the correction, not the 1/(n-1) form or the gamma value. The paper never estimates a dilution exponent. The evidence comes from EC meeting attendance and only loosely fits multi-year office co-tenure. It also shows a live inconsistency: the sidecar dilutes by headcount and the scored operator does not.

bearings.paper_claim: Core measures computed on the clique expansion diverge from hypergraph-native hypercoreness. The authors say a hypergraph representation is 'more than a minor modeling choice'.
bearings.system_side: PageRank (d 0.7/0.85/0.95) and the component eigenvector run on row-normalized co-tenure strengths, which are pairwise edges derived from container co-presence. Containers are grouping layers, not hyperedges in the operator.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper compares coreness, not PageRank, so it only implies that walk-based ranks on a projection may diverge from a hypergraph treatment. Under D-025 the ranks are heuristic outputs, not access measures, in either representation.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-staffer-network#Layer-balanced PageRank, eigenvector and bridging diversity|Layer-balanced PageRank, eigenvector and bridging diversity]]

bearings.paper_claim: Large hyperedges inflate attendees' centrality when projected to cliques, yet those large hyperedges are what connects the network (edge betweenness correlates 0.74 with size).
bearings.system_side: Stage 3 builds sponsor-to-cosponsor ties per bill and multiplies each by sizenorm_factor(C) with SIZE_NORM = 'sqrt' (1/sqrt(C)). That discounts big multi-cosponsor bills without removing them. The engine reads the resulting Edges sheet and mean-symmetrizes it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports discounting by hyperedge size, a bill-level discount, as distinct from the REJECTED per-member volume normalization. It gives no basis for 1/sqrt(C) over log or 1/C. A bill roster is an asynchronous set of signatures with sponsor direction, not a simultaneous meeting. The data are EC lobbying meetings, not US House cosponsorship.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Cosponsorship network construction|Cosponsorship network construction]]

bearings.paper_claim: Core-periphery and rich-club claims are tested against hypergraph configuration null models (Chodrow 2020) that preserve degree and edge size, using rho(k) = phi(k)/phi_rand(k). Stakeholders show rho > 1 for all k. Large meetings drive connectivity.
bearings.system_side: The sector diagnostic flags hub concentration with a fixed rule: 'dominated' if hub degree >= 3x the second-highest. Crypto is recorded as one 167-degree star (the CBDC cosponsor roster, which is a single large bill) against 25 for second place, with cascade reach 33 from the hub vs 7.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A null-model rich-club or core test would show whether a sector's concentration exceeds what its degree and bill-size sequence already implies. The 3x rule cannot separate that. This only holds if sector bill rosters are treated as hyperedges. With the thin samples (crypto p_max 0.23), null-model variance will be large. Any result is UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: No component represents group events as hyperedges. Cosponsor rosters, payroll containers and interview episodes are all clique- or star-projected, so no hypergraph-native core or centrality is available for comparison.

The staffer co-tenure operator still has no container-size treatment (OPEN ruling at build_staffer_social_network.py:222-234), even though the sidecar exposure index already divides by headcount. The paper's clique-inflation result bears directly on that ruling.

Concentration and core claims in the sector diagnostics use an ad hoc 3x-hub rule, with no degree- and size-preserving null model. The system cannot say whether a sector's rich-club or core structure exceeds what its degree sequence implies.

No core-periphery or k-core decomposition exists for any Melange graph. Core composition by actor category (party, chamber, committee, staffer role), as the paper does for stakeholder types, is not computed.

Multi-edge treatment (repeated co-sponsorship or repeated co-tenure versus binarized ties) is not reported as a sensitivity axis. The paper shows its core fragments at higher orders when repeated meetings are kept.
There is no US contact register comparable to the EC meetings register, so a lobbyist-to-office contact network cannot be built from disclosure data (D-021 holds).
flags: D-025 wording conflict: Paul highlighted the Discussion sentence (p.10) that core-periphery structures show a concentration of 'access and influence'. If imported, that reading would make graph ranks or core membership into access or influence claims, which D-025 bars. The paper itself says centrality does not directly measure influence (p.10) and that the resource links are not causal (p.9).

Near-collision with REJECTED proposal (2), per-edge volume normalization: the paper's preference for analysis without multi-edges (p.5-6), and any reading of its clique-inflation result as 'down-weight each edge', resemble the measured-and-rejected per-edge normalization (STATE.md:912-915). Katz sums over edges, so per-edge reweighting cannot remove a degree artifact. The paper's remedy is a hypergraph-native measure, not edge reweighting. Do not cite it as support for per-edge volume normalization.
Container-size normalization in the staffer operator is an OPEN owner ruling. This paper is evidence for that ruling, not authorization to apply it.
Any null-model or hypercore analysis run on Melange graphs from this paper is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Every figure quoted from the paper must keep its window and denominator: EC disclosed meetings, 1 Dec 2019 to 30 Nov 2024; regression N = 1,178 companies (H) and 702 (Hstak). These are EC stakeholders, not US legislators.
LDA must not be used to build a meeting-style edge layer by analogy with this paper (D-021).
paul_alignment: Paul's markup on this paper is highlights only, with no notes. The highlights favour the rich-club coefficient, the hypergraph argument, determinants of centrality (the FTE finding), and the Discussion claim of concentrated 'access and influence'. The evidence agrees with his standing position that more research on forms of centrality is needed. The hypercoreness vs clique-coreness divergence is exactly that kind of result. It also fits the system's 2026-06-25 retirement of direction-blind centrality, and the paper's own caveat that centrality is not influence backs that retirement. His highlight of the 'access and influence' sentence is the one point that would conflict with D-025 if transferred, so treat it as the authors' interpretive claim, not a property of Melange ranks. His notes do not connect the paper to the staffer network. Its sharpest bearing is there, on the open container-size ruling and the degree vs office-size r = 0.87 record, which his notes predate.

related.why: Bacik measures the US LDA lobbying network over time, while Azaiez measures the EC meeting network. Together they contrast a disclosure regime without named officials (LDA) with one that names both parties to each contact (EC register).
Both build networks from lobbying data via bipartite or group affiliation and study community or core structure among interest groups.
Porter projects committee co-membership, a bipartite or hyperedge structure, onto a weighted graph. Azaiez shows how such projections distort core measures compared with a hypergraph treatment.

Sotoudeh builds a cosponsorship network, the clique or star projection of bill rosters that the system's 1/sqrt(C) size discount follows, and finds eigenvector centrality a weak predictor of passage. Azaiez gives the general reason projected centrality misleads.
Ringe et al. propose co-voting centrality as a measure of political influence. Azaiez states that centrality measures embeddedness and not influence directly.
Azaiez's NGO shared-meeting and coalition reading (p.7-8, p.10) draws on the coalition literature that Pritoni reviews, including the 'coalitions as weakness' argument.

Battaglini and Patacchini price legislators by Katz-Bonacich centrality. Azaiez finds that interest-group resources predict the groups' own centrality, the reverse side of the same access market (the system's kb_benchmark is diagnostic only).

extraction.doi: 10.1016/j.jpubeco.2025.105451 (printed in the PDF). Metadata hint said 10.2139/ssrn.4892936 and PII S0047272725001495; neither appears in the extracted text, so they are unverified. Use the journal DOI.
extraction.document_type: Journal article: empirical political economy (descriptive record-linkage analysis, donor-candidate regressions, counterfactual voucher simulation)
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in four chunks (lines 1-1696, pp. 1-14 including references). Appendix figures and tables (A2-A7, incl. A4-A6 panel results and A6/A7 ideology and wealth figures) are cited but NOT in the extracted text. Data availability: on request. Paul's 63 highlights all fall on pp. 1-13; none carry note text.
extraction.research_question: How unequal is money in US politics across generations, and does this inequality affect political representation? (a) Age distribution of donors, voters, candidates and officeholders; (b) whether donors give more often and more per gift to candidates closer to their age; (c) whether seed (early) fundraising depends on candidate age; (d) how a voucher policy would change candidate fundraising by age.
extraction.theory: Resource-based account of participation (Brady, Verba and Schlozman 1995) applied to age: generational wealth gaps (life-cycle and cohort effects, Gale et al. 2020) produce contribution gaps, which shape the candidate pipeline through campaign money as a selectorate (early seed money from personal networks; Bonica 2017, 2020) and access (Kalla and Broockman 2016; Austen-Smith 1995). Alternative explanations (public demand/taste-based discrimination, population demographics, electoral institutions; Sec. 1, pp. 2-3) are argued to be less likely drivers. Campaign finance is positioned as one important driver, not the sole one (p. 3).
extraction.data: (1) FEC itemized individual contributions from DIME v4.0: over 600 million itemized donations 1979-2020, most 2016-2020; 23 million unique donor IDs; record linkage links 75% of individual contributors who gave in the 2012-2020 cycles, about 17 million donors (Sec. 3.2, p. 5). (2) L2 national voter file snapshot (April 2021): about 208 million registered voters, with date of birth, primary and general turnout history; census age estimates adjust for unregistered and non-citizen populations (Sec. 3.1, p. 4; fn. 8). (3) Candidate birth years for 11,741 congressional candidates 2012-2020 from congressional bios, Project Vote Smart, and L2 linkage; linkage correlation with Vote Smart r = 0.95 (Sec. 3.3, p. 5; fn. 11). Main donor analyses focus on the 2020 cycle because small-donor coverage (ActBlue, WinRed) is near-complete then (Sec. 3, p. 4). Unit and N by table: Table 1 candidate-cycle, N = 6,098 candidates (2012-2020, at least 10 donors per cycle); Tables 2-3 donor-candidate pairs in 2020: Democrats 2,048,581,125 pairs (Donated outcome) and 6,945,203 (asinh amount); Republicans 829,871,280 and 3,964,488; Table 4 non-incumbent House candidates in 2020, N = 931 (challengers and open seats); seed funding uses each candidate first 50 donations. Panel robustness (appendix) about 200 million same-state dyads, 2012-2020.
extraction.method: Descriptive: age distributions for 2020 (box plots, medians and dollar-weighted means), generational shares of wealth vs donations (Fig. 6), and birth-cohort representational weight = cohort share of contributions over population share, scaled to 18-year-olds = 1 (Fig. 4). Candidate-level OLS (Eq. 1): average donor age (or dollar-weighted average) on candidate age x incumbency, with cycle and district fixed effects (Table 1). Donor-level linear probability model (Donated x100) and asinh(amount) (Eq. 2): |Age Gap| between donor and candidate, same-state control, donor and candidate two-way fixed effects, separately for Democrats and Republicans, with generation interactions (Tables 2-3; text p. 8-9). Seed-funding OLS with district fixed effects (Table 4). Counterfactual voucher simulation (Sec. 6.1, pp. 12-13): post-stratification reweighting of contributions so that strata (birth year, precinct partisanship in 10 groups, population density in 5 bins) match electoral shares, via inflation factor eta_s = electoral share / contribution share; gamma_c = voucher-program contributions / actual contributions per candidate; log(gamma_c) plotted by candidate age with loess (Fig. 8).
extraction.identification: No exogenous policy shock. Within-district variation (Table 1, district FE) and within-donor / within-candidate variation (Eq. 2, two-way FE; donor and candidate fixed effects absorb time-invariant donor and candidate traits, incl. wealth and ideology). Authors state they do not estimate the wealth elasticity or the causal effect of wealth or of policy (pp. 1-2) and call exogenous policy variation future work (Sec. 7). Eq. 2 relies on the age gap varying across donor-candidate pairs within a donor; the text does not test time-varying dyad confounds. Voucher results are a counterfactual reweighting under stated assumptions, not an estimate.
extraction.scope: US federal elections (House and Senate candidates and their individual donors), mainly the 2020 cycle; panel robustness 2012-2020 in appendix (same-state dyads only). Population: near-universe of voters (L2), donors (DIME-linked), and candidates. Era: 2012-2020 data, with 2020 as the core cycle. Institution: post-Citizens United, post-McCutcheon US campaign finance (individual limit $2,900 per election cited on p. 11). Not covered: PAC, party and presidential money (excluded in Fig. 5); dark money (explicitly not accounted for, Sec. 6, p. 11).

key_findings.finding: Median dollar of campaign contributions comes from a 66-year-old; mean dollar from a 64-year-old (63.9); median unweighted donor is 59. Only 9% of contribution dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger.
key_findings.numbers: median dollar 66; mean dollar 63.9; median donor 59; 9% of dollars from donors <=40

key_findings.finding: Age gaps in participation: median voter 52, median non-voter 39, median primary voter 59. Average American age 38; voting-age public age 47. Candidates slightly younger than donors; incumbents slightly older. Those gaps are smaller than the gap between donors and general-election voters or non-voters.
key_findings.numbers: voters 52; non-voters 39; primary voters 59; donors 59; US average 38; voting-age public 47

key_findings.finding: Generational shares of donations track wealth shares. Baby Boomers give 53.6% of donation dollars and receive 48.5% of candidate receipts; Millennials give 5% of donation dollars and receive 10.4% of candidate receipts. Millennial candidates get over 66% of their dollars from Silent and Boomer donors plus about 20% from Gen X; Millennial donors supply 4% of Boomer candidates' receipts.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.1 p. 7 (Fig. 6); Sec. 4.1 p. 6 and Appendix A7 for wealth shares
key_findings.numbers: Boomer donors 53.6%; Millennial donors 5%; Millennial candidate receipts 10.4%; Millennial candidates 66%+ from Silent/Boomers; Gen X ~20%; Millennial share of Boomer-candidate money 4%; wealth shares Millennials 4.5%, Boomers 53.1%; contributions Millennials 5.3%, Boomers 52.8%

key_findings.finding: Representational weight rises sharply with age. 35-year-olds are over 25 times better represented than 18-year-olds; the most represented cohorts (ages 70-80) give about 200-300 times more per capita than the youngest cohort.
key_findings.numbers: 35-year-olds >25x 18-year-olds; ages 70-80 200-300x youngest cohort per capita

key_findings.finding: Average contribution size rises with donor birth cohort. Donors born after 1985 give about $75 on average; donors born 1940-1965 about $200; pre-1935 cohorts about $300. Ever-donors to the $2,900 limit average 63 years old.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.1 / Fig. 5 p. 6 and Sec. 6 p. 11
key_findings.numbers: post-1985 ~$75; 1940-1965 ~$200; pre-1935 ~$300; limit-donors average age 63

key_findings.finding: Candidate age is strongly associated with donor age within districts. Each year of candidate age raises average donor age by about 0.21 years (unweighted) and dollar-weighted donor age by about 0.20 years. Donor-age SD is 5.8 vs 12.5 for candidate age. Incumbents have donors about 8 years older on average (unweighted).
key_findings.numbers: 0.21 (SE 0.01); 0.20 (SE 0.01); N = 6,098 candidate-cycles; incumbent +8.16 years; SD donor age 5.8, candidate age 12.5

key_findings.finding: Within-donor, two-way fixed-effects estimates: donors are less likely to give, and give less, the larger the age gap with a candidate. Paper reports that a 30-year age gap is associated with about a 50% reduction in the likelihood of donating (baseline 0.189 for Democrats, 0.184 for Republicans, x100 scale). Effects are similar across parties on the extensive margin.
key_findings.numbers: Democrats extensive |Age Gap| coef -0.00328 (SE 0.00001); Republicans -0.00317 (SE 0.00003); intensive asinh(amount) Democrats -0.00178 (SE 0.00005), Republicans -0.00218 (SE 0.00008); baseline donating rate 0.189 (D) and 0.184 (R); 30-year gap ~50% lower donation likelihood (authors' calculation)

key_findings.finding: Generation interactions: the age-gap penalty on donating is largest for the oldest and youngest donors (Silent generation -0.00502 for Democrats). For Gen Z, a larger age gap strongly lowers donating but conditional on donating, Gen Z donors give slightly more to more distant-age candidates (Democrats +0.00132; Republicans +0.00335 on the intensive margin, which the text describes as the same pattern).
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.3 p. 9 and fn. 14 p. 9; Tables 2-3
key_findings.numbers: Silent x age gap -0.00502 (D); Gen Z x age gap -0.00332 extensive (D); Gen Z intensive +0.00132 (D), +0.00335 (R)

key_findings.finding: Effect is more pronounced for Democrats, where donor age varies more and ideology is more age-polarized (abstract and Sec. 5.3). Republican coefficients are unexpectedly positive in cycles before 2020, which the authors attribute to lower Republican donor-age variance and missing small donors before WinRed.
key_findings.location: Intro p. 2; Sec. 5.3 p. 9; fn. 3 p. 2; fn. 3 text pp. 2-3
key_findings.numbers: Pre-2020 Republican age-gap coefficients positive; Democratic coefficients similar 2014-2018 and smaller in 2012

key_findings.finding: Seed funding (first 50 donations) is older-donor heavy for older candidates. Within district, a 65-year-old's seed donors are 8.4 years older than a 35-year-old's. Each year of candidate age adds about $6.91 to average seed-donor amount (a 65- vs 35-year-old raises about $207 more per early donor). Older candidates self-fund more, about 6% more per year of age.
key_findings.numbers: seed donor age coef 0.28 (SE 0.02) per year; $6.91 (SE 1.67) per year; ln(self-funding) 0.06 (SE 0.01); N = 931; R2 0.58, 0.46, 0.43; 8.4-year and $207 differences for 35 vs 65

key_findings.finding: Voucher simulation (4 x $25-type credits in Seattle comparison; simulated full participation matching voter turnout): the average candidate under age 30 would raise over three times more funds; candidates over 66 raise less on average, down to about one-third fewer for the average candidate over 80. Threshold age is 66. Intro states the average candidate under 50 would get about twice the share of contributions and candidates below 66 benefit on average.
key_findings.numbers: threshold age 66; under 30 >3x; over 80 about 1/3 fewer; under 50 ~2x share of contributions; example gamma AOC (b. 1989) 2.05; Barbara Lee (b. 1946) and Jamie Raskin (b. 1962) below 0.5

key_findings.finding: Underrepresented young subgroup in the simulation: older Millennials (b. 1985-1989) in Democratic-leaning, high-density districts are 1.45% of the 2020 electorate but only 0.96% of contributions; the simulation raises their share to 1.45%.
key_findings.numbers: 1.45% electorate vs 0.96% of contributions

key_findings.finding: Authors reject taste-based age discrimination by voters as the main driver: conjoint studies show public favors younger candidates, over 70% back maximum age limits, and constituent approval is negatively associated with age net of ideology. Party age distributions are close (House Democrats avg 59, Republicans 57). US legislators are the oldest in the OECD, while the correlation between population median age and legislator age across countries is -0.003.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1 pp. 2-3; Fig. 1 p. 2 caption; intro p. 1
key_findings.numbers: correlation -0.003; over 70% support age limits; Congress avg age 58 House, 64 Senate (2022); Democrats 59, Republicans 57

key_findings.finding: Donor-candidate linkage is near-representative: linked and unlinked donors show similar retired/student shares; unlinked donors have slightly more conservative CFscores and larger average donations, which the authors do not treat as material bias.
key_findings.numbers: 75% linked; 17 million linked donors; birth year validation r = 0.95

key_findings.finding: Abstract claims older donors are much more ideologically conservative than younger donors, and that donor-partisanship age gaps exceed those in voting and survey attitudes. The text body does not give the supporting numbers (they are in appendix figures not extracted).
key_findings.location: Highlights p. 1; abstract/intro p. 1-2; Sec. 4 (Appendix A6)
key_findings.numbers: not in extracted main text

limitations: Paper states it does not directly estimate wealth elasticities or causal effects of wealth or contributions; cited causal evaluation of policy left to future work with exogenous changes (pp. 1-2; Sec. 7).

Small-donor coverage: data before 2020 exclude most small donors (ActBlue and WinRed itemization; Sec. 3 p. 4; fn. 3; Sec. 5.3 p. 9). Pre-2020 Republican coefficients are unexpectedly positive and the party comparison is only clean for 2020.
Dark money (Citizens United-era independent groups) is not accounted for (Sec. 6 p. 11).
Extensive-margin models use donor fixed effects, so non-donors drop out of that estimate (Sec. 5.3 p. 8). Panel robustness (2012-2020) restricted to same-state dyads (about 200 million observations).

Record linkage links 75% of donors; misses occur for different addresses, unregistered donors and name changes. Linkage algorithm designed to limit false positives, which can bias the linked sample (Sec. 3.2 pp. 4-5).

Voucher simulation assumes full participation with donor shares matched to voter turnout, all candidates adopt vouchers and cannot take private money, and simple assumptions about spending and candidate pipelines (intro p. 2; Sec. 6.1 pp. 11-13; fn. 16). Informational costs of vouchers may reduce young participation (Sec. 6 p. 11). Contribution-limit age effects are described as less certain (Sec. 6 p. 11).
Seed-funding model uses only non-incumbent House candidates in 2020 (N = 931) with district fixed effects and no candidate fixed effects (Sec. 5.4 p. 10).

Authors cannot rule out alternative theories of contribution behavior, e.g., political efficacy and inclusion (fn. 2 p. 2). Online small-dollar strategies by younger candidates are an alternative explanation for seed-funding gaps (fn. 15 p. 11).
Cohort vs life-cycle effects are not separately identified in the main analysis; text says generational patterns are interpreted with both (Sec. 1, Sec. 7).
Data available only on request (Data availability statement). Appendix figures and tables (A2-A7) not in the extracted text, so appendix-only claims were not verified.
Reference-list mismatch: text cites (Li, 2022) for online scams, but the reference list has Zhao, L., 2022 (Lemons in the political marketplace). Treat that citation as unverified.

summary_md:
Bonica and Grumbach link DIME itemized FEC contributions to the L2 voter file and to candidate birth years. They show that US federal campaign money is much older than the electorate. In the 2020 cycle, the median contribution dollar comes from a 66-year-old, the median donor is 59, and only 9% of dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger. For comparison, the median general-election voter is 52, the median primary voter is 59 and the median non-voter is 39. Within districts, each year of candidate age adds about 0.21 years to average donor age (N = 6,098 candidate-cycles, 2012-2020). Within donors, using two-way fixed effects on 2020 donor-candidate pairs, a larger age gap lowers the chance of giving. The authors put a 30-year gap at about a 50% lower donating rate. The coefficient is -0.00328 for Democrats and -0.00317 for Republicans on a x100 scale. Pre-2020 Republican estimates are unstable because of WinRed coverage. Seed money, defined as the first 50 donations, is older and larger for older non-incumbent House candidates (N = 931). A voucher reweighting, which is a counterfactual and not an estimate, would raise funds for candidates under 66. The paper is descriptive and states that it identifies no causal effect of wealth or of policy.

For Paul's systems, its main use is as a measurement warning, not as an engine parameter. Terrier's Sphere and Participation standings run on vendor fields for political giving and turnout. The paper shows both are steeply age-graded. Terrier stratifies standings by registration but not by age, so its top deciles will lean older. Mentat's identity ladder and conduit handling line up with the paper's own data hazards: linkage built to avoid false positives, and small-donor itemization that is only complete from 2020. The paper does not bear on the Moneyball ranking, the cascade engine or the SNA layers.
